transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi… yeah, thanks for seeing me. I guess what finally made me make the appointment is that I’ve been having more trouble keeping my place with normal work things. I’m a receptionist, so I’m scheduling appointments and keeping track of little details all day, and lately I’ll be in the middle of entering something or arranging the lobby displays, and it’s like my mind just slips off track.

It’s not that I don’t know how to do the work or anything. I’ll start thinking, “Did I forget to tell someone something?” or “What if I overlooked that note?” and then I lose where I was. Then I have to back up and check again, sometimes more than once, and it’s just been bothering me enough that I thought I should talk to someone about it.
When those thoughts like “Did I forget to tell someone something?” pop up, do they feel intrusive and hard to dismiss?

Yeah… intrusive is a good word for it, I think. It’s like I can tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled, you already did that,” and for maybe a second I believe it, but then the thought just sort of comes back around again. Like it doesn’t feel settled.

And it’s not always just the one thing, either. I’ll start with, “Did I pass that message along?” and then it turns into, “What if I put the appointment in the wrong place?” or “What if I missed some little detail and someone’s going to be upset later?” And then I’m mentally going back through the steps, almost replaying them, checking them in my head over and over. I know it’s not really helping after a certain point, but it’s hard to just drop it and move on.
When those doubts come up, do you find yourself checking your work again and again?

Yes… I do, but it’s a little tricky, because sometimes it’s not even that I physically go back and check the computer or the paper every single time. Sometimes I do that, definitely, like I’ll re-open the appointment or look back at a note I already know I read. But a lot of the time it’s more like I’m checking it in my head over and over.

I’ll tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled, you already did that,” and I’ll try to move on, but the thought doesn’t really stay put. It loops back. And then I start going from one thing to the next, like first I’m worried I didn’t enter something correctly, then I’m thinking maybe I forgot to pass along a message, and then I’m remembering some tiny detail from earlier and wondering if I missed that too.

So yes, I guess I am checking again and again, just sometimes it’s mental checking more than anything. And it feels frustrating because I know after a point I’m not actually finding anything new, I’m just trying to get that settled feeling, and I don’t really get it.
When that unsettled feeling shows up, do you feel like you have to keep checking until it feels completely certain?

Yeah… I think that’s pretty close to what happens. It’s not like I sit there thinking, “I need absolute certainty,” in those words, but that’s kind of what I’m reaching for. I’ll tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled, you already did that,” and I do mean it in the moment. I’m trying to be reasonable with myself.

But then the thought doesn’t really stay gone. It loops back around, and then it’s like I’m not just checking the original thing anymore. I start with one concern, like whether I put something in correctly, and then suddenly I’m thinking about whether I passed along a message, or whether I missed some little note, or whether there was another detail I should have caught. And before I know it, I’m going through all these steps in my head over and over.

I think I’m trying to get to that feeling of, “Okay, yes, everything is definitely fine,” but I don’t always get there. Or if I do, it doesn’t last very long. It’s frustrating, because part of me knows I’ve already checked, or at least thought it through, but it still feels unsettled enough that I keep circling back.
Do these repeated doubts feel unreasonable to you, even while you’re having them?

Yes… I mean, a lot of the time I can tell it’s probably unreasonable, or at least bigger than the situation really calls for. Like, logically I know a small paperwork mistake at work is usually just a small mistake. Or if a schedule gets a little mixed up, it can usually be fixed. But in my head it starts feeling like, “Well, what if this turns into a whole bigger problem?” Like one little thing could snowball somehow.

And it’s not just work, honestly. I catch myself doing it with ordinary things too—bills, travel plans, schedules, little details that most people would probably check once and move on from. I’ll be thinking, “Did I pay that on time?” or “What if I misunderstood the plan?” or “What if I wrote something down wrong?” And even while I’m thinking it, there’s this part of me that knows, Sunny, you’re making this heavier than it needs to be. But that doesn’t always make it stop.

So yes, I do see that the doubts are often not… I don’t know, not proportionate, I guess. But in the moment they still feel important enough that I can’t quite let them go.
About how much time do these checking thoughts and mental reviewing take up in a typical day?

It’s hard to put an exact number on it, because it’s not always like I sit down and check for one solid hour or something. It’s more broken up through the day. I’ll have a few minutes where I’m going over one thing, then I move on, then it pops back in again, and I’m mentally reviewing it while I’m trying to do something else.

On a typical day, I’d say maybe… I don’t know, maybe half an hour total? Sometimes more if it’s a busy day or if there were a lot of details to keep track of. It can feel like more than that because it keeps interrupting me. Like I can tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled, you already did that,” but then the thought keeps looping back anyway. And then pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another, and I’m checking details in my head over and over.

So it’s not all day, exactly. I can still do my work and get through things. But it does take up enough time and attention that I notice it, and it wears on me.
Do these thoughts feel like unwanted intrusions, rather than the kind of worries you see as justified by real-life problems?

I guess… yes and no. They do feel unwanted, in the sense that I’m not sitting there choosing to think about these things for fun. I’ll be trying to get through my day, and then suddenly I’m worrying about a work schedule, or whether I paid a bill, or whether I made some little paperwork error that’s going to come back and cause a bigger problem.

But at the same time, they don’t always feel completely random, if that makes sense. It’s usually tied to something real, like a bill or a travel plan or a detail at work. It’s just that my mind takes an ordinary thing and treats it like it could turn into some much larger mess. Like one small mix-up won’t just be inconvenient—it’ll somehow snowball. So part of me feels like, “Well, I’m being responsible, I should think about this,” and another part of me knows I’m going way past what the situation probably needs.

So I wouldn’t say they feel justified exactly. They feel like regular life worries that get too big and too sticky, and then I can’t quite put them down.
Besides going over things in your mind, do you also find yourself repeatedly checking things in a physical way?

I’m not sure I’d say repeatedly in a big way. I mean, I do normal checking, like making sure the door is locked or looking at an email before I send it, but I don’t think I’m going back over and over physically the way I do in my head.

Most of it is more mental for me. Like I might remember that I already looked at something, but then I’ll keep replaying whether I looked carefully enough, if that makes sense. I’m not usually standing there checking the stove ten times or anything like that. It’s more that I’ll review it internally and sort of try to reassure myself that it was handled.

I guess if I’m really unsure, I might look once more—like checking a bill payment confirmation or a calendar entry—but I don’t think it’s a major physical checking routine. It’s more the thinking afterward that gets sticky.
If you try not to go over it again in your mind, what does it feel like will happen?

It feels like… if I don’t go over it, then I’m leaving something unfinished, even if I technically know I already handled it. Like there’s this uncomfortable loose end in my mind. I can tell myself, “Sunny, you already checked that, it’s fine, move on,” but it doesn’t really settle. The thought just sort of comes back around, like, “Are you sure? What if you missed one detail?”

And then if I try to ignore it, I feel like I’m taking a risk, even though I know that sounds a little dramatic for the kinds of things I’m talking about. It’s not usually some huge crisis. It’s more like a schedule, a bill, a message, a small work detail. But my mind acts like if I don’t review it again, something could slip through and then I’ll have to deal with the consequences later.

The frustrating part is that it doesn’t stay with just one thing. I’ll start by trying not to think about one concern, and then another one pops up, and pretty soon I’m mentally checking several things. So even when I know it’s handled, the thought keeps looping, and I end up going over details in my head again just to try to feel sure.
Did these worries and mental checking start after a specific stressful event or change in your life?

Yes… I think it did start after something specific. It’s been about nine months now, give or take, and it really seemed to begin after that overnight detention and the whole paperwork mix-up around it.

I don’t know if I connected it right away, because at first I think I was just telling myself, “Well, of course I’m stressed, that was a bad experience,” and I was trying to just get back to normal. But when I look back, that’s when this pattern of second-guessing and going back over details really started to feel more constant. Before that, I could worry, sure, but it didn’t have this same… sticky quality to it.

And the paperwork part of it especially, I think, made me feel like one mistake or one missing detail could turn into something much bigger than it should. So now when anything involves forms, schedules, bills, confirmations—anything where there’s a record or some official detail—I notice my mind goes right back to that feeling. But yes, the short answer is that it’s been going on for about nine months, since that incident and the paperwork mix-up connected to it.
Do these thoughts ever feel like they pull you back into that detention incident, as if you’re reliving it?

I’m not sure I’d describe it as reliving it, exactly. I mean, I do think about it, and sometimes the worry sort of points back to it, especially if something reminds me of paperwork or making sure something is documented correctly. But it’s more like I’m worrying about making another mistake or missing something, not like I’m suddenly back there in the moment.

I don’t usually feel like I’m physically in that situation again, if that’s what you mean. It’s more that the memory kind of sits in the background and gives the current worry more weight. Like my mind says, “Remember what happened when something wasn’t handled right?” But I wouldn’t say I’m seeing it happen again or feeling like I’m actually there.

So… no, not really reliving it. More replaying the meaning of it, if that makes sense.
When you go over these details in your mind, does it feel like something you have to do to relieve the anxiety?

Yes… it does feel like I have to do it, even when I know that doesn’t totally make sense. It’s like if I don’t go over the details, the anxiety just sits there and keeps poking at me. I can tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled, you already dealt with it,” but the thought doesn’t really listen to that. It keeps looping back around.

And then I’ll start with one thing, like, “Did I send that message correctly?” or “Did I remember that appointment?” and before I know it, I’m onto another concern and then another one. It’s almost like my brain starts making a little list without me meaning to. So I end up checking details in my head over and over, trying to get that feeling of certainty.

It does relieve the anxiety a little bit, but only for a short time. Then the doubt creeps back in, and I feel pulled to review it again. That’s the part that bothers me, because I’m not doing it because I want to sit there thinking about all these things. I’m doing it because it feels like I won’t be able to relax unless I do.
Do you avoid reminders of the detention incident?

I’m not sure I’d say I avoid reminders in a really clear way. I mean… I don’t think I’m going out of my way to avoid anything connected to it, at least not that I’ve noticed. It’s more that when something does remind me of it, I get uncomfortable and I start thinking more about whether everything is in order.

Like, if there’s paperwork or official-looking forms or anything where I have to double-check details, I might feel that little tightening feeling, but I don’t think I’m avoiding those things entirely. I still deal with them if I have to. Maybe I’m a little slower with them, or I feel more tense, but I wouldn’t say I’m steering clear of reminders on purpose.

So… I guess the honest answer is I haven’t really noticed avoidance so much as feeling uneasy when reminders come up.
While you’re doing the mental checking, does part of you feel it’s excessive or doesn’t really make sense?

Yes, part of me knows it’s excessive. I can kind of hear myself thinking, Sunny, this is handled, you already checked it, you don’t need to keep going over it. But the problem is that knowing that doesn’t make the thought stop.

It’s like there’s the reasonable part of me that can see I’m circling, and then there’s the anxious part that keeps saying, But what if you missed something? What if you’re remembering it wrong? So I’ll try to move on, but then the thought loops right back around, and pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another. I might start out checking one detail in my head, and then suddenly I’m reviewing three or four other things too.

So yes, I do recognize that it doesn’t really make sense to keep doing it as much as I do. It just feels hard to stop once it gets going, because the checking feels like the only way to calm it down, even if only for a little while.
When you go over things in your mind, do you feel you have to do it in a particular way until it feels just right?

I don’t think it’s in a particular way, exactly. Not like I have to count things or repeat a phrase a certain number of times, or do it in some exact order until it feels perfect. It’s more… I get stuck reviewing it, but it’s not very organized.

Like, I’ll go back over what happened or what I said or whether I forgot something, and I’m trying to get that settled feeling, but I don’t think there’s a special routine to it. Sometimes I’ll start in the middle of the thought, then jump backward, then jump to another detail, so it’s not like there’s one correct sequence I have to follow. It’s more that I keep circling until I feel a little calmer, or until I get tired of it, honestly.

So… if you mean, do I have a rule in my head like, “I have to think it through this exact way or it doesn’t count,” then no, I haven’t really noticed that. It’s more about trying to reassure myself that I didn’t miss anything.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about many different parts of life, even when there isn’t a specific detail to check?

Yes… yes, I do. It’s not always tied to one specific thing I can point to and say, “This is what I need to check.” A lot of the time it’s more like my mind is scanning for what could go wrong.

It can be ordinary things, too, which is what feels frustrating. Like at work, I’ll worry about the schedule or whether I misunderstood something small. At home it might be bills, or whether I planned something correctly, or if there’s some little paperwork error I didn’t catch. Even travel plans—just basic things like times, reservations, directions—I can start imagining that one small mix-up is going to snowball into a much bigger problem.

And I know these are normal parts of life that everyone deals with, but I seem to give them more weight than they deserve. It’s like my mind treats a small loose end as if it could turn into a serious issue if I don’t stay on top of it. So yes, it’s definitely not just one detail. It spreads across a lot of different everyday things.
Do you find it hard to control the worrying, even when you’re not mentally checking or reviewing things?

Yes, I do. Even when I’m not sitting there deliberately reviewing something, the worry still feels hard to shut off. I can tell myself, Sunny, it’s handled, there’s nothing else to do right now, but the thought doesn’t really listen to that.

It’ll keep looping in the background, and then before I realize it, I’ve moved from one concern to another. I might start with one small thing, like whether I understood a detail correctly, and then suddenly I’m thinking about something else I might have forgotten, and then another thing after that. It’s like my brain keeps looking for the next possible problem.

And I know I’m trying to reassure myself, but it doesn’t always work. I’ll think, Okay, that’s fine, move on, and then a few minutes later I’m back checking the details in my head again, even if I didn’t mean to start doing that. It’s not always this huge panic feeling or anything, but it’s persistent. It just keeps tugging at me.
Do these thoughts ever feel alien or not like your own mind, rather than just excessive worry?

No, I don’t think they feel alien exactly. I mean, they feel like my thoughts — just too many of them, and too hard to quiet down.

It’s not like a thought pops in and I think, “That isn’t me,” or like it feels put there by someone else. It’s more that I recognize the worry as coming from me, from my own mind, but I also feel frustrated because I can’t seem to make it stop when I want to. So it’s familiar, just… overactive, I guess.

Sometimes I’ll even know I’m being excessive while it’s happening, like part of me is saying, “You’re probably making too much of this,” but the worry still keeps going. So no, I wouldn’t call it alien. It feels like my own mind getting stuck on things.
Over the past several months, have you often felt physically tense or keyed up?

Yes… I think that’s actually one of the main ways it shows up for me. I can be at the front desk doing my job, smiling, answering phones, helping people, acting normal on the outside, and inside I feel completely wound tight.

It’s like my shoulders are always creeping up toward my ears, and I don’t even notice until I suddenly realize I’m sitting there all stiff. I’ll try to relax them, and then a few minutes later they’re right back up again. It’s not necessarily that anything terrible is happening in that exact moment, but my body feels like I’m waiting for something to go wrong — like I need to be ready to catch a mistake or respond to some problem.

And because I’m in a receptionist role, I’m used to being pleasant and composed, so I think I hide it pretty well. People probably wouldn’t look at me and think I’m tense. But inside, yes, I feel keyed up a lot of the time. Not in a dramatic way, more like this steady tightness that’s just there in the background.
When you start mentally reviewing things, does it feel like something you have to do to make the anxiety go down?

Yes… I think that’s a fair way to put it. It’s not always like I consciously decide, “I need to review this now,” but once the anxiety starts, my mind sort of reaches for reviewing as a way to calm it down.

Like I’ll tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled, you already dealt with that,” and for a second I might feel like I can move on. But then the thought keeps looping anyway, like it’s not satisfied. So I’ll go back over the detail again in my head, just to make sure I’m remembering it right or that I didn’t miss something. And then that leads to another concern, and then another one, and pretty soon I’ve spent all this time checking things mentally over and over.

I guess it does feel like I’m doing it to make the worry go down, but it doesn’t really work for long. It might quiet it for a moment, but then my brain finds another angle to worry about. So yes, it feels like something I’m pulled into doing, even when I know it’s not really helping.

Yeah… I think that’s pretty close to what happens. It’s not like I sit there thinking, “I need absolute certainty,” in those words, but that’s kind of what I’m reaching for. I’ll tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled, you already did that,” and I do mean it in the moment. I’m trying to be reasonable with myself.

But then the thought doesn’t really stay gone. It loops back around, and then it’s like I’m not just checking the original thing anymore. doctor.question: Do these repeated doubts feel unreasonable to you, even while you’re having them?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I find myself worrying about all kinds of ordinary things now—work schedules, bills, travel plans, even little paperwork errors—as if one small mix-up could turn into a much bigger problem.

patient.answer:
Yes… I mean, a lot of the time I can tell it’s probably unreasonable, or at least bigger than the situation really calls for. Like, logically I know a small paperwork mistake at work is usually just a small mistake. Or if a schedule gets a little mixed up, it can usually be fixed. But in my head it starts feeling like, “Well, what if this turns into a whole bigger problem?” Like one little thing could snowball somehow.

And it’s not just work, honestly. I catch myself doing it with ordinary things too—bills, travel plans, schedules, little details that most people would probably check once and move on from. I’ll be thinking, “Did I pay that on time?” or “What if I misunderstood the plan?” or “What if I wrote something down wrong?” And even while I’m thinking it, there’s this part of me that knows, Sunny, you’re making this heavier than it needs to be. But that doesn’t always make it stop.

So yes, I do see that the doubts are often not… I don’t know, not proportionate, I guess. But in the moment they still feel important enough that I can’t quite let them go.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the intrusive doubts and mental checking are time-consuming enough to support OCD over generalized anxiety or other causes.
doctor.question: About how much time do these checking thoughts and mental reviewing take up in a typical day?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I can tell myself, ‘Sunny, it’s handled,’ but the thought keeps looping, and pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another until I’m checking details in my head over and over.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about how much time is spent in repeated checking thoughts and mental reviewing, which most directly reflects the looping, hard-to-control worry described in this symptom profile.

patient.answer:
It’s hard to put an exact number on it, because it’s not always like I sit down and check for one solid hour or something. It’s more broken up through the day. I’ll have a few minutes where I’m going over one thing, then I move on, then it pops back in again, and I’m mentally reviewing it while I’m trying to do something else.

On a typical day, I’d say maybe… I don’t know, maybe half an hour total? Sometimes more if it’s a busy day or if there were a lot of details to keep track of. It can feel like more than that because it keeps interrupting me. Like I can tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled, you already did that,” but then the thought keeps looping back anyway. And then pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another, and I’m checking details in my head over and over.

So it’s not all day, exactly. I can still do my work and get through things. But it does take up enough time and attention that I notice it, and it wears on me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions versus excessive real-life worry, to distinguish OCD from generalized anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: Do these thoughts feel like unwanted intrusions, rather than the kind of worries you see as justified by real-life problems?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I find myself worrying about all kinds of ordinary things now—work schedules, bills, travel plans, even little paperwork errors—as if one small mix-up could turn into a much bigger problem.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the thoughts are ordinary real-life worries that have become excessive, rather than intrusive obsessional thoughts.

patient.answer:
I guess… yes and no. They do feel unwanted, in the sense that I’m not sitting there choosing to think about these things for fun. I’ll be trying to get through my day, and then suddenly I’m worrying about a work schedule, or whether I paid a bill, or whether I made some little paperwork error that’s going to come back and cause a bigger problem.

But at the same time, they don’t always feel completely random, if that makes sense. It’s usually tied to something real, like a bill or a travel plan or a detail at work. It’s just that my mind takes an ordinary thing and treats it like it could turn into some much larger mess. Like one small mix-up won’t just be inconvenient—it’ll somehow snowball. So part of me feels like, “Well, I’m being responsible, I should think about this,” and another part of me knows I’m going way past what the situation probably needs.

So I wouldn’t say they feel justified exactly. They feel like regular life worries that get too big and too sticky, and then I can’t quite put them down.

doctor.intent: Differentiate OCD-style obsessions/compulsions from generalized anxiety by determining whether the patient engages in overt, repetitive checking behaviors beyond mental reviewing.
doctor.question: Besides going over things in your mind, do you also find yourself repeatedly checking things in a physical way?

target_item.reason: The question asks about repeated physical checking behaviors, but the provided symptom profile only covers mental reviewing, worry, tension, sleep, concentration, impairment, and duration, not physical checking compulsions.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d say repeatedly in a big way. I mean, I do normal checking, like making sure the door is locked or looking at an email before I send it, but I don’t think I’m going back over and over physically the way I do in my head.

Most of it is more mental for me. Like I might remember that I already looked at something, but then I’ll keep replaying whether I looked carefully enough, if that makes sense. I’m not usually standing there checking the stove ten times or anything like that. It’s more that I’ll review it internally and sort of try to reassure myself that it was handled.

I guess if I’m really unsure, I might look once more—like checking a bill payment confirmation or a calendar entry—but I don’t think it’s a major physical checking routine. It’s more the thinking afterward that gets sticky.

doctor.intent: Differentiate obsessive intrusive doubts with mental compulsions from generalized worry by assessing ego-dystonicity and feared consequences if the person resists the checking.
doctor.question: If you try not to go over it again in your mind, what does it feel like will happen?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I can tell myself, ‘Sunny, it’s handled,’ but the thought keeps looping, and pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another until I’m checking details in my head over and over.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking what happens internally when trying not to mentally review the concern, which most directly relates to difficulty stopping or controlling the worry.

patient.answer:
It feels like… if I don’t go over it, then I’m leaving something unfinished, even if I technically know I already handled it. Like there’s this uncomfortable loose end in my mind. I can tell myself, “Sunny, you already checked that, it’s fine, move on,” but it doesn’t really settle. The thought just sort of comes back around, like, “Are you sure? What if you missed one detail?”

And then if I try to ignore it, I feel like I’m taking a risk, even though I know that sounds a little dramatic for the kinds of things I’m talking about. It’s not usually some huge crisis. It’s more like a schedule, a bill, a message, a small work detail. But my mind acts like if I don’t review it again, something could slip through and then I’ll have to deal with the consequences later.

The frustrating part is that it doesn’t stay with just one thing. I’ll start by trying not to think about one concern, and then another one pops up, and pretty soon I’m mentally checking several things. So even when I know it’s handled, the thought keeps looping, and I end up going over details in my head again just to try to feel sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the anxiety and checking are linked to a recent identifiable stressor, which would help distinguish adjustment disorder from OCD/GAD.
doctor.question: Did these worries and mental checking start after a specific stressful event or change in your life?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about nine months, ever since that overnight detention and the paperwork mix-up around it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking when the worries and mental checking began and whether they followed a specific stressful event, which is covered by the duration item noting it has been going on for about nine months since the overnight detention and paperwork mix-up.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think it did start after something specific. It’s been about nine months now, give or take, and it really seemed to begin after that overnight detention and the whole paperwork mix-up around it.

I don’t know if I connected it right away, because at first I think I was just telling myself, “Well, of course I’m stressed, that was a bad experience,” and I was trying to just get back to normal. But when I look back, that’s when this pattern of second-guessing and going back over details really started to feel more constant. Before that, I could worry, sure, but it didn’t have this same… sticky quality to it.

And the paperwork part of it especially, I think, made me feel like one mistake or one missing detail could turn into something much bigger than it should. So now when anything involves forms, schedules, bills, confirmations—anything where there’s a record or some official detail—I notice my mind goes right back to that feeling. But yes, the short answer is that it’s been going on for about nine months, since that incident and the paperwork mix-up connected to it.

inference.note: Onset after a specific stressful event 9 months ago following detention/paperwork mix-up increases relevance of F43.22, while persistent intrusive doubts with mental checking/need for certainty still strongly support F42.9. No clear evidence this turn to rule out F41.1, F33.1, or F90.0.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are specifically trauma-linked re-experiencing rather than generalized worry or OCD-type obsessions, to distinguish adjustment disorder from the other candidates.
doctor.question: Do these thoughts ever feel like they pull you back into that detention incident, as if you’re reliving it?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about trauma-related re-experiencing or reliving the detention incident, which is not covered by the listed Generalized Anxiety Disorder symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d describe it as reliving it, exactly. I mean, I do think about it, and sometimes the worry sort of points back to it, especially if something reminds me of paperwork or making sure something is documented correctly. But it’s more like I’m worrying about making another mistake or missing something, not like I’m suddenly back there in the moment.

I don’t usually feel like I’m physically in that situation again, if that’s what you mean. It’s more that the memory kind of sits in the background and gives the current worry more weight. Like my mind says, “Remember what happened when something wasn’t handled right?” But I wouldn’t say I’m seeing it happen again or feeling like I’m actually there.

So… no, not really reliving it. More replaying the meaning of it, if that makes sense.

inference.note: Removed F33.1 and F90.0. This turn supports onset after a stressor with persistent worry/mental checking, but the patient denies reliving phenomena, making PTSD less likely. The intrusive, repetitive, ego-dystonic mental checking remains most consistent with OCD; adjustment disorder and GAD remain in the differential.

doctor.intent: Differentiate obsessive unwanted thoughts from generalized excessive worry by testing whether the mental reviewing is performed to neutralize anxiety and resist an urge, which would support OCD over GAD or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: When you go over these details in your mind, does it feel like something you have to do to relieve the anxiety?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I can tell myself, ‘Sunny, it’s handled,’ but the thought keeps looping, and pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another until I’m checking details in my head over and over.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the repeated mental reviewing feels difficult to resist and is used to reduce anxiety, which most directly matches uncontrollable worry and mental checking.

patient.answer:
Yes… it does feel like I have to do it, even when I know that doesn’t totally make sense. It’s like if I don’t go over the details, the anxiety just sits there and keeps poking at me. I can tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled, you already dealt with it,” but the thought doesn’t really listen to that. It keeps looping back around.

And then I’ll start with one thing, like, “Did I send that message correctly?” or “Did I remember that appointment?” and before I know it, I’m onto another concern and then another one. It’s almost like my brain starts making a little list without me meaning to. So I end up checking details in my head over and over, trying to get that feeling of certainty.

It does relieve the anxiety a little bit, but only for a short time. Then the doubt creeps back in, and I feel pulled to review it again. That’s the part that bothers me, because I’m not doing it because I want to sit there thinking about all these things. I’m doing it because it feels like I won’t be able to relax unless I do.

doctor.intent: Differentiate OCD from anxiety related to a traumatic/stressful event by assessing avoidance of reminders of the detention incident.
doctor.question: Do you avoid reminders of the detention incident?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoidance of reminders of the detention incident, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d say I avoid reminders in a really clear way. I mean… I don’t think I’m going out of my way to avoid anything connected to it, at least not that I’ve noticed. It’s more that when something does remind me of it, I get uncomfortable and I start thinking more about whether everything is in order.

Like, if there’s paperwork or official-looking forms or anything where I have to double-check details, I might feel that little tightening feeling, but I don’t think I’m avoiding those things entirely. I still deal with them if I have to. Maybe I’m a little slower with them, or I feel more tense, but I wouldn’t say I’m steering clear of reminders on purpose.

So… I guess the honest answer is I haven’t really noticed avoidance so much as feeling uneasy when reminders come up.

doctor.intent: Differentiate OCD from generalized anxiety/adjustment disorder by testing whether the patient recognizes the mental reviewing as excessive or senseless in the moment, a key feature supporting obsessions/compulsions.
doctor.question: While you’re doing the mental checking, does part of you feel it’s excessive or doesn’t really make sense?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I can tell myself, ‘Sunny, it’s handled,’ but the thought keeps looping, and pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another until I’m checking details in my head over and over.
target_item.reason: The question is about recognizing that the mental checking may be excessive while still feeling unable to stop it, which best matches difficulty controlling the worry and repeated checking in my head.

patient.answer:
Yes, part of me knows it’s excessive. I can kind of hear myself thinking, Sunny, this is handled, you already checked it, you don’t need to keep going over it. But the problem is that knowing that doesn’t make the thought stop.

It’s like there’s the reasonable part of me that can see I’m circling, and then there’s the anxious part that keeps saying, But what if you missed something? What if you’re remembering it wrong? So I’ll try to move on, but then the thought loops right back around, and pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another. I might start out checking one detail in my head, and then suddenly I’m reviewing three or four other things too.

So yes, I do recognize that it doesn’t really make sense to keep doing it as much as I do. It just feels hard to stop once it gets going, because the checking feels like the only way to calm it down, even if only for a little while.

doctor.intent: Differentiate OCD from generalized anxiety or adjustment disorder by determining whether the mental checking follows rigid rules or rituals rather than ordinary worry.
doctor.question: When you go over things in your mind, do you feel you have to do it in a particular way until it feels just right?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a ritualized or 'just right' quality to mental checking, which is not specifically covered by the listed GAD symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I don’t think it’s in a particular way, exactly. Not like I have to count things or repeat a phrase a certain number of times, or do it in some exact order until it feels perfect. It’s more… I get stuck reviewing it, but it’s not very organized.

Like, I’ll go back over what happened or what I said or whether I forgot something, and I’m trying to get that settled feeling, but I don’t think there’s a special routine to it. Sometimes I’ll start in the middle of the thought, then jump backward, then jump to another detail, so it’s not like there’s one correct sequence I have to follow. It’s more that I keep circling until I feel a little calmer, or until I get tired of it, honestly.

So… if you mean, do I have a rule in my head like, “I have to think it through this exact way or it doesn’t count,” then no, I haven’t really noticed that. It’s more about trying to reassure myself that I didn’t miss anything.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the worries are pervasive and difficult to control across many areas of life rather than primarily obsessional checking/rumination tied to a specific feared mistake pattern.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself worrying excessively about many different parts of life, even when there isn’t a specific detail to check?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I find myself worrying about all kinds of ordinary things now—work schedules, bills, travel plans, even little paperwork errors—as if one small mix-up could turn into a much bigger problem.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worry is excessive and spread across many different areas of life, which directly matches excessive anxiety and worry about a number of events or activities.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I do. It’s not always tied to one specific thing I can point to and say, “This is what I need to check.” A lot of the time it’s more like my mind is scanning for what could go wrong.

It can be ordinary things, too, which is what feels frustrating. Like at work, I’ll worry about the schedule or whether I misunderstood something small. At home it might be bills, or whether I planned something correctly, or if there’s some little paperwork error I didn’t catch. Even travel plans—just basic things like times, reservations, directions—I can start imagining that one small mix-up is going to snowball into a much bigger problem.

And I know these are normal parts of life that everyone deals with, but I seem to give them more weight than they deserve. It’s like my mind treats a small loose end as if it could turn into a serious issue if I don’t stay on top of it. So yes, it’s definitely not just one detail. It spreads across a lot of different everyday things.

doctor.intent: Differentiate generalized anxiety disorder from OCD by determining whether the worry is difficult to control across the day, independent of compulsive mental checking.
doctor.question: Do you find it hard to control the worrying, even when you’re not mentally checking or reviewing things?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I can tell myself, ‘Sunny, it’s handled,’ but the thought keeps looping, and pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another until I’m checking details in my head over and over.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worry is difficult to control even outside of mental checking or reviewing, which directly matches uncontrollable worry.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do. Even when I’m not sitting there deliberately reviewing something, the worry still feels hard to shut off. I can tell myself, Sunny, it’s handled, there’s nothing else to do right now, but the thought doesn’t really listen to that.

It’ll keep looping in the background, and then before I realize it, I’ve moved from one concern to another. I might start with one small thing, like whether I understood a detail correctly, and then suddenly I’m thinking about something else I might have forgotten, and then another thing after that. It’s like my brain keeps looking for the next possible problem.

And I know I’m trying to reassure myself, but it doesn’t always work. I’ll think, Okay, that’s fine, move on, and then a few minutes later I’m back checking the details in my head again, even if I didn’t mean to start doing that. It’s not always this huge panic feeling or anything, but it’s persistent. It just keeps tugging at me.

doctor.intent: Differentiate generalized worry from obsessional mental compulsions by testing whether the patient experiences the thoughts as ego-dystonic and alien versus ordinary excessive worry.
doctor.question: Do these thoughts ever feel alien or not like your own mind, rather than just excessive worry?

target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the thoughts feel alien or not like the patient’s own mind, which is not covered by the listed GAD symptom profiles. The profiles describe excessive and uncontrollable worry, but not alien or externally experienced thoughts.

patient.answer:
No, I don’t think they feel alien exactly. I mean, they feel like my thoughts — just too many of them, and too hard to quiet down.

It’s not like a thought pops in and I think, “That isn’t me,” or like it feels put there by someone else. It’s more that I recognize the worry as coming from me, from my own mind, but I also feel frustrated because I can’t seem to make it stop when I want to. So it’s familiar, just… overactive, I guess.

Sometimes I’ll even know I’m being excessive while it’s happening, like part of me is saying, “You’re probably making too much of this,” but the worry still keeps going. So no, I wouldn’t call it alien. It feels like my own mind getting stuck on things.

inference.note: Current turn supports generalized, hard-to-control worry across multiple domains and thoughts experienced as ego-syntonic/own mind, which makes F41.1 strongest; however persistent anxiety-relieving mental checking with insight still keeps F42.9 in the differential. Trauma-linked onset remains present but lack of re-experiencing/avoidance keeps F43.22 lower rather than ruling it out.

doctor.intent: Differentiate generalized anxiety disorder from adjustment disorder by determining whether the patient has the characteristic associated physical symptoms of generalized anxiety.
doctor.question: Over the past several months, have you often felt physically tense or keyed up?

target_item.name: Restlessness_Tension
target_item.manifestation: At the front desk I can still smile and help people, but inside I feel wound tight, like my shoulders are up around my ears and I’m waiting for something to go wrong.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling physically tense or keyed up over the past several months, which directly matches restlessness/tension.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think that’s actually one of the main ways it shows up for me. I can be at the front desk doing my job, smiling, answering phones, helping people, acting normal on the outside, and inside I feel completely wound tight.

It’s like my shoulders are always creeping up toward my ears, and I don’t even notice until I suddenly realize I’m sitting there all stiff. I’ll try to relax them, and then a few minutes later they’re right back up again. It’s not necessarily that anything terrible is happening in that exact moment, but my body feels like I’m waiting for something to go wrong — like I need to be ready to catch a mistake or respond to some problem.

And because I’m in a receptionist role, I’m used to being pleasant and composed, so I think I hide it pretty well. People probably wouldn’t look at me and think I’m tense. But inside, yes, I feel keyed up a lot of the time. Not in a dramatic way, more like this steady tightness that’s just there in the background.

doctor.intent: Differentiate OCD from generalized or adjustment-related anxiety by clarifying whether the repetitive mental reviewing is experienced as a compulsion performed to neutralize anxiety rather than ordinary worry.
doctor.question: When you start mentally reviewing things, does it feel like something you have to do to make the anxiety go down?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I can tell myself, ‘Sunny, it’s handled,’ but the thought keeps looping, and pretty soon I’ve gone from one concern to another until I’m checking details in my head over and over.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about the mental reviewing/checking and whether it feels driven by anxiety, which most directly relates to the difficulty stopping or controlling worry.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think that’s a fair way to put it. It’s not always like I consciously decide, “I need to review this now,” but once the anxiety starts, my mind sort of reaches for reviewing as a way to calm it down.

Like I’ll tell myself, “Sunny, it’s handled, you already dealt with that,” and for a second I might feel like I can move on. But then the thought keeps looping anyway, like it’s not satisfied. So I’ll go back over the detail again in my head, just to make sure I’m remembering it right or that I didn’t miss something. And then that leads to another concern, and then another one, and pretty soon I’ve spent all this time checking things mentally over and over.

I guess it does feel like I’m doing it to make the worry go down, but it doesn’t really work for long. It might quiet it for a moment, but then my brain finds another angle to worry about. So yes, it feels like something I’m pulled into doing, even when I know it’s not really helping.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The presentation is most consistent with generalized anxiety disorder: persistent, hard-to-control excessive worry across multiple everyday domains for about 9 months, with associated physical tension/keyed-up feeling and noticeable interference at work. Although there is repetitive mental reviewing/checking, the thoughts are largely excessive real-life worries rather than clearly distinct obsessions, and the checking appears secondary to anxiety reduction rather than a classic OCD syndrome. Symptoms began after a stressful event, but there is no evidence of trauma re-experiencing or avoidance sufficient for a trauma-related disorder; the chronic, generalized worry pattern is more consistent with GAD than adjustment disorder.
